parts:
Dear Brittany,

I think that it's not wrong to fit an N-mixture model to all zeroes and ones, but I still tried your data as an occupancy model (function occu()).  I tried the simplest one, but did not succeed, see below. One thing which is extreme in your data set is the temporal replication. I have never seen 82 temporal reps before. I would consider lumping some of your days or else fitting perhaps a dynamic occupancy model (function colext). However, with so few detections overall (11 ones, versus 1219 zeroes), you are likely to run into trouble with almost any kind of hierarchical occupancy or abundance model perhaps.

Regards  --  Marc

Dear all,

of course I am a big fan of BUGS (though you ran JAGS, which is even better perhaps ;)), but, this data set is very problematic in principle: with such extremely small detection probability, the occupancy model is well known to often yield positive biases in occupancy, and often very much so, see the simulations in the original occupancy paper (MacKenzie et al., Ecology, 2002).

Regards  --  Marc

parts:
Just a quick update.  Marc was successful in that his estimates on the logit scale do correspond to the maximum likelihood estimates for the probability of presence and the detection probability as 1 and 11/(15*82), respectively.

A brute force maximization of the log likelihood for the model with the logit of the detection probability being a + b*temperature gives maximum likelihood estimates of the probability of presence being 1 (same as with the basic occupancy model) and a-hat = -6.78022 and b-hat = 0.0337441 with AIC = 129.368 (just slightly lower than 129.673, the AIC value for the basic occupancy model).  Estimates asymptotic standard errors for a-hat and b-hat are 1.5349 and 0.02333, respectively.

Jim

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Re: Error: Hessian is singular. Try using fewer covariates.
parts:
Dear Brittany,

I have a couple of general comments on the choice of "the best method for analysis". I feel that the choice of an analytical method depends on at least three things: ecology, sample design and biology of your species, and available analytical resources.
(1) To decide what is the best method to analyse a set of data you must start from the ecological question. Without a clear idea of "why" you want to do an analysis, there is no way to say what analysis is best or even adequate. I see this as the same thing as the "why-what-how" progression of questions in monitoring (Yoccoz et al, TREE, 2001).
(2) Even if you want to analyse your data a certain way, perhaps your data were not collected such that you can reasonably make the assumptions implicit in the use of a certain model, or, the way how your species behaves (for instance, moves in space and time) does not match the assumptions of the model.
(3) The best possible method may not be within your reach because the model or the fitting may be too complicated for you to understand, for instance, if you'd have to code up some complicated MCMC algorithm.
Consideration of all three aspects may lead you to conclude that a certain model is best for your question, your design/your species and for your resources. In some cases, it may even lead to the conclusion that no reasonable analysis is possible for your data set.

More specifically, in your case, you seem to be interested in spatial and potentially temporal patterns in a bird population around a lake, and you worry about imperfect detection, hence you use the mixed models in unmarked rather than those you can fit in lme4, for instance. Ideally, you might analyse the counts and model abundance, but in the bittern case, with max counts of one, you can do occupancy with hardly any loss of information.

One important assumption for occupancy models is closure: that the state of occurrence of a site ("species present" or "species absent") does not change over the duration of your sampling. With a large number of occasions, this assumption is always suspect, and with your sampling extending over 3 years, is bound to be violated so strongly, in my opinion, to make the analysis meaningless.

So you must account for the openness of the system, by considering a dynamic occupancy model perhaps (function colext) or, if you want to model counts for estimation of abundance, use dynamic N-mixture models (i.e., the Dail-Madsen model, pcountOpen). Remember that the closure assumption is (much) more difficult to meet when modeling abundance, rather than occurrence, because a change in the abundance state from one occasion to another from 8 to say 7, means a violation of the closure assumption when modeling abundance, but not when modeling occurrence (i.e., occupancy).

However, in your case, with such sparse data (15 bittern detections  or so ?), using the more complex dynamic model (with more params to estimate) would "dilute" the little information you have so much more that it would most likely fail as well for numerical reasons.

So in my opinion, for the bittern, you just don't have enough data to do any reasonable modeling in unmarked, and you should take other species with (many) more observed birds.

(((Or, some people (actually many) would simply forget about modeling measurement errors (= 1 minus detection prob) and model the observed occurrence using some kind of logistic regression perhaps. This approach comes with a couple of important hidden assumptions, which may or may not screw your inference, and you simply don't know it: (1) detection is perfect or (2) detection is not perfect but at least does not vary along desired dimensions of comparisons, e.g., does not vary much between habitat types along the lake, which you are interested in comparing.)))

Kind regards --  Marc
